options.label: Yes — all modern databases automatically split hot partitions
options.description: Automatic hot spot handling is a standard database feature

options.label: Yes — hash partitioning automatically prevents all hot spots
options.description: Hash functions guarantee even load distribution

explanation.reasoning: As of DDIA's writing, most databases cannot automatically detect and compensate for hot keys. It remains the application's responsibility to identify hot keys and apply mitigation (random suffixes, caching, etc.). Automatic hot spot detection and redistribution is an area of ongoing research but is not yet a standard feature in production databases.
explanation.tradeoffs: Some systems provide tools to help — monitoring dashboards, per-partition metrics — but the actual mitigation logic must be implemented by the application. Future databases may handle this automatically, but for now, it's a manual concern that must be designed into the application architecture.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Hot key detection and mitigation is currently an application-level responsibility. Most databases don't automatically redistribute hot keys — it's an open area of research.
explanation.commonMistake: Assuming the database will automatically handle hot keys. Application architects must plan for celebrity/hot key scenarios and implement mitigation strategies proactively.

prompt.context:
You operate an IoT platform with 100,000 sensors writing data every second. The partition key is timestamp (key-range partitioning). All writes go to today's partition.

You consider three fixes:
- A: Hash partition by timestamp
- B: Change key to (sensor_id, timestamp) with key-range partitioning
- C: Change key to (sensor_id, timestamp) with hash on sensor_id only
prompt.question: Which fix eliminates the write hot spot while preserving efficient per-sensor time-range queries?

options.label: C — hash sensor_id across partitions, sort by timestamp within each partition
options.description: Writes are spread by sensor_id; time-range queries for one sensor scan sorted data within one partition

options.label: A — hash partitioning by timestamp distributes writes evenly
options.description: Hashing timestamps ensures even write distribution

options.label: B — key-range on (sensor_id, timestamp) preserves sort order
options.description: Key-range partitioning with compound key maintains time ordering

explanation.reasoning: Option C (Cassandra-style compound key) hashes sensor_id to distribute writes across partitions — each sensor lands on a different partition. Within each partition, data is sorted by timestamp, enabling efficient time-range queries for a specific sensor. Option A hashes timestamps, destroying time ordering. Option B key-range on compound key would still have skew if sensor_id ranges are uneven.
explanation.tradeoffs: Option C sacrifices cross-sensor time-range queries (scatter/gather) for per-sensor efficiency. This is acceptable if per-sensor queries dominate. If you need 'all sensors at time T,' you'd need a secondary index or a separate materialized view.
explanation.keyTakeaway: The Cassandra-style compound key (hash first component, sort by rest) solves the write hot spot while preserving per-partition range queries — the best compromise for most time-series workloads.
explanation.commonMistake: Thinking key-range partitioning on a compound key is always safe. If the first component (sensor_id) has skewed access patterns, key-range still concentrates popular sensors on one partition. Hashing the first component is safer for distribution.

prompt.context:
Your car sales database is partitioned by document ID. Each partition stores a subset of car listings.

A user searches: 'all red cars.' The color field is NOT the partition key.

Each partition maintains its OWN secondary index on color, covering only the listings in that partition.
prompt.question: How is this query executed?

options.label: Scatter/gather: send the query to ALL partitions, each searches its local index, results are combined
options.description: Every partition's local index must be queried because red cars could be on any partition

options.label: A single partition's index has all color data — the query is routed there
options.description: One partition stores the global color index

options.label: The query fails — secondary index queries aren't supported on partitioned databases
options.description: Only primary key queries work with partitioning

explanation.reasoning: With document-partitioned (local) secondary indexes, each partition independently indexes only its own data. A query on 'color=red' can't know which partitions have red cars, so it must be sent to ALL partitions. Each partition searches its local color index and returns matching documents. The results from all partitions are then combined. This is called scatter/gather.
explanation.tradeoffs: Local indexes make writes simple — when you add a car listing, only one partition's index needs updating. But reads by secondary index require scatter/gather across all partitions, which is expensive. This is also known as 'document-partitioned' indexing.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Document-partitioned (local) secondary indexes: each partition indexes its own data. Writes are local (fast), but secondary index queries require scatter/gather across all partitions.
explanation.commonMistake: Assuming a secondary index query on a partitioned database only hits one partition. With local indexes, EVERY partition must be queried because the secondary index data is distributed.

prompt.context:
Your scatter/gather query hits 20 partitions in parallel. 19 partitions respond in 5ms, but one partition is under heavy load and responds in 500ms.

The overall query latency is 500ms — determined by the slowest partition.
prompt.question: What is this latency problem called?

options.label: Tail latency amplification — the response time is determined by the slowest partition (the tail of the latency distribution)
options.description: With N parallel requests, the chance of hitting at least one slow response increases with N

options.label: Head-of-line blocking — the first response blocks the rest
options.description: Results are processed sequentially, with the first result blocking

options.label: Partition skew — one partition has more data than others
options.description: The slow partition has more documents to search

explanation.reasoning: Tail latency amplification occurs when a request fans out to multiple services (or partitions) in parallel and the overall latency is determined by the slowest response. Even if 99th percentile latency per partition is 500ms, with 20 parallel requests, the probability that at least one exceeds 500ms is much higher. More partitions = worse tail latency.
explanation.tradeoffs: This is a fundamental problem with scatter/gather. Mitigations include: reducing the number of partitions queried (using global indexes instead), hedging requests (sending to multiple replicas), or setting timeouts and returning partial results. But the fundamental amplification effect can't be eliminated.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Scatter/gather amplifies tail latency: the overall response time equals the slowest partition. More partitions = more chances to hit a slow one.
explanation.commonMistake: Evaluating scatter/gather performance using average latency. The median may be fine, but the p99 is much worse because tail latency amplification compounds with each additional partition.

prompt.context:
Your car listings database supports two query patterns:
1. Search by make + model (e.g., 'Toyota Camry') — these always include the partition key (make)
2. Search by color across all makes (e.g., 'all red cars')

Data is partitioned by make. Each partition has local secondary indexes on color, model, year, etc.
prompt.question: For which query pattern are local secondary indexes efficient?

options.label: Query 1 — when the partition key is included, the query targets a single partition's local index
options.description: Searching 'Toyota Camry' routes to the Toyota partition and uses its local index on model

options.label: Query 2 — color searches benefit from local indexes across all partitions
options.description: Local indexes make cross-partition color searches efficient

options.label: Both are equally efficient with local secondary indexes
options.description: Local indexes optimize all secondary key lookups equally

explanation.reasoning: When the query includes the partition key ('make=Toyota'), it routes to a single partition. That partition's local secondary index on 'model' then efficiently finds 'Camry'. No scatter/gather needed. But 'all red cars' (no partition key) requires scatter/gather across ALL partitions — much more expensive. Local indexes are efficient when queries usually include the partition key.
explanation.tradeoffs: This is why partition key choice is so important. If most queries include the partition key, local indexes work great (single-partition lookups). If most queries filter by secondary attributes WITHOUT the partition key, you're doing scatter/gather on every query — consider a global index instead.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Local secondary indexes are efficient when queries include the partition key (single-partition lookup). Without the partition key, every query becomes scatter/gather.
explanation.commonMistake: Choosing a partition key without considering secondary index query patterns. If most queries don't include the partition key, local indexes cause expensive scatter/gather on every search.

prompt.context:
You're reviewing how various databases handle secondary indexes in a partitioned/sharded setup:

- MongoDB
- Riak
- Cassandra
- Elasticsearch / SolrCloud
- VoltDB
prompt.question: What approach do these databases use for secondary indexes?

options.label: Document-partitioned (local) secondary indexes with scatter/gather for non-partition-key queries
options.description: Each shard maintains its own local index; cross-shard queries use scatter/gather

options.label: A single global index stored on a dedicated node
options.description: One node holds the entire secondary index for all partitions

options.label: These databases don't support secondary indexes at all
options.description: Secondary indexes are not available in partitioned mode

explanation.reasoning: MongoDB, Riak, Cassandra, Elasticsearch, SolrCloud, and VoltDB all use document-partitioned (local) secondary indexes. Each partition/shard maintains its own secondary index covering only its data. Queries on secondary fields that don't include the partition key require scatter/gather — known as a 'global query' in MongoDB or a 'scatter-gather query' in other systems.
explanation.tradeoffs: Local indexes are the most common approach because they keep writes simple (only one partition's index needs updating). The read-side scatter/gather cost is accepted as a trade-off. Elasticsearch and Solr are search engines built around this pattern — they're optimized for parallel scatter/gather with sophisticated result merging.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Document-partitioned (local) secondary indexes are the dominant approach in distributed databases: MongoDB, Riak, Cassandra, Elasticsearch, SolrCloud, and VoltDB all use this pattern.
explanation.commonMistake: Expecting secondary index queries on these databases to be as fast as primary key lookups. Secondary queries require scatter/gather, which is fundamentally more expensive.

prompt.context:
Instead of each partition maintaining its own color index, you build a GLOBAL secondary index on color that is itself partitioned:

- Partition 0 of the color index: colors a-r (covers 'red')
- Partition 1 of the color index: colors s-z (covers 'silver')

The color index partition is stored separately from the data partitions.

A user queries: 'all red cars.'
prompt.question: How does the query execute with this global (term-partitioned) secondary index?

options.label: Route to the single index partition for 'red' (partition 0), get the list of document IDs, then fetch those documents from their respective data partitions
options.description: One index lookup, then targeted fetches — no scatter/gather on the index

options.label: Scatter the query to all data partitions, same as with local indexes
options.description: Global indexes still require scatter/gather for reads

options.label: The global index returns the full documents directly, no further fetches needed
options.description: The index stores complete copies of all matching documents

explanation.reasoning: With a term-partitioned (global) secondary index, the query 'color=red' routes to the specific index partition that covers 'red.' That partition returns a list of document IDs matching the color. The system then fetches those documents from their respective data partitions. The key advantage: the index lookup hits ONE partition, not all of them — reads are efficient.
explanation.tradeoffs: The trade-off is on writes: when you add a red car to data partition 5, the global color index (on a different partition) also needs updating. A single document write may require updating indexes on multiple partitions — a distributed write that's more complex and slower than local index updates.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Global (term-partitioned) secondary indexes make reads efficient (single index partition lookup) at the cost of more complex writes (updating index entries across partition boundaries).
explanation.commonMistake: Thinking a global secondary index is stored on a single node. It's partitioned too — but partitioned by the INDEX term (e.g., color value), not by the same key as the data.

prompt.context:
When a new car listing (red Toyota, partition 5) is inserted, the global color index (on partition 0) must be updated to include this new document.

This is a cross-partition write: the data goes to partition 5, but the index update goes to partition 0.
prompt.question: Why are global secondary index updates usually asynchronous?

options.label: Synchronous cross-partition updates would require distributed transactions, adding significant latency and complexity
options.description: Updating index and data partitions atomically requires 2PC or equivalent, which is expensive

options.label: Asynchronous updates are more accurate because they can batch changes
options.description: Batching produces better index quality than real-time updates

options.label: Network bandwidth between partitions is too limited for synchronous updates
options.description: The volume of index update traffic would saturate the network

explanation.reasoning: A synchronous global index update means: write data to partition 5 AND update the index on partition 0 in a single atomic transaction. This requires a distributed transaction (like two-phase commit) which adds latency, complexity, and reduces availability. Instead, most systems update global secondary indexes asynchronously — the index may be slightly stale but writes are fast and simple.
explanation.tradeoffs: The consequence of async updates: a read on the global index immediately after a write may not reflect the latest change. Amazon DynamoDB's global secondary indexes are async and state that updates are reflected 'within a fraction of a second' under normal conditions — but there's no hard guarantee.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Global secondary index updates are usually asynchronous because synchronous cross-partition updates would require expensive distributed transactions. The trade-off is temporary index staleness.
explanation.commonMistake: Expecting a global secondary index query to reflect a write that just completed. With async index updates, there's a brief window where the index is stale — read-after-write consistency is not guaranteed.

prompt.context:
You're designing the partitioning scheme for a global secondary index on car color. Two options:

- A: Partition the index by term range (a-r on partition 0, s-z on partition 1)
- B: Partition the index by hash of the term (hash('red') → partition 3, hash('silver') → partition 7)
prompt.question: What is the trade-off between these approaches?

options.label: Range: efficient range scans on the index term (e.g., all colors starting with 'r') but risk of hot spots. Hash: even distribution but no range scans.
options.description: Same key-range vs hash trade-off applies to the index itself

options.label: Range is always faster because it avoids hash computation
options.description: Avoiding the hash function overhead makes range partitioning faster

options.label: Hash is always better because global indexes need even distribution
options.description: Global indexes must be hash-partitioned to work correctly

explanation.reasoning: The same key-range vs hash trade-off from data partitioning applies to global index partitioning. Range-partitioned indexes support efficient range scans on the index term (e.g., 'all cars with colors between red and russet') but can have hot spots if certain terms are much more popular. Hash-partitioned indexes distribute terms evenly but destroy ordering — range scans on the term require scatter/gather.
explanation.tradeoffs: For a global index on price, range partitioning enables efficient queries like 'all cars between $10K and $20K.' For an index on color (where range scans are rare), hash partitioning's even distribution is more valuable. Choose based on whether range queries on the INDEX term are important.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Global secondary indexes can be partitioned by term range (enables range scans) or hash of term (even distribution). The same key-range vs hash trade-off applies.
explanation.commonMistake: Forgetting that global secondary indexes are partitioned too — and the partitioning strategy for the INDEX is a separate decision from the data partitioning strategy.

prompt.context:
You're choosing between local and global secondary indexes for your partitioned database:

| Aspect | Local (Document) | Global (Term) |
|--------|-----------------|---------------|
| Write  | ?               | ?             |
| Read   | ?               | ?             |
prompt.question: Which correctly describes the read/write trade-off?

options.label: Local: fast writes (single partition), slow reads (scatter/gather). Global: slow writes (cross-partition), fast reads (single index partition).
options.description: Local optimizes writes; global optimizes reads

options.label: Local: slow writes, fast reads. Global: fast writes, slow reads.
options.description: Local optimizes reads; global optimizes writes

options.label: Both have the same read/write performance characteristics
options.description: The indexing strategy doesn't affect read/write trade-offs

explanation.reasoning: Local (document-partitioned) indexes: writes are fast because only one partition's index needs updating. But reads by secondary index require scatter/gather across all partitions. Global (term-partitioned) indexes: reads are efficient (single index partition lookup). But writes are more complex because the data partition and index partition may be different nodes, requiring cross-partition updates (usually async).
explanation.tradeoffs: This is the fundamental trade-off between the two approaches. If your workload is write-heavy and reads usually include the partition key, local indexes are better. If reads by secondary attributes are the dominant pattern, global indexes provide much better read performance at the cost of write complexity and index staleness.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Local secondary indexes optimize for write simplicity (single-partition writes) but pay at read time (scatter/gather). Global secondary indexes optimize for read efficiency (single-partition lookup) but pay at write time (cross-partition updates).
explanation.commonMistake: Choosing between local and global indexes without understanding the workload. The right choice depends on whether reads or writes dominate, and whether queries typically include the partition key.

prompt.context:
Your cluster has grown from 4 to 6 nodes. Some nodes have more data than others due to organic growth. You need to move data so that load is shared fairly across all 6 nodes.

Requirements:
- After rebalancing, load should be spread fairly
- During rebalancing, reads and writes should continue working
- Only the minimum necessary data should move between nodes
prompt.question: What is this process called?

options.label: Rebalancing — moving data between nodes to maintain fair distribution as the cluster changes
options.description: The process of redistributing partitions across nodes after cluster size or data volume changes

options.label: Repartitioning — changing the partition boundaries to split data differently
options.description: Modifying how data is divided into partitions

options.label: Defragmentation — compacting data within each node
options.description: Reorganizing data on disk for better performance

explanation.reasoning: Rebalancing is the process of moving partitions between nodes to maintain fair load distribution. It's needed when: nodes are added or removed, data grows unevenly, or throughput increases requiring more nodes. The key requirements are: (1) fair distribution afterward, (2) continued service during the process, (3) minimal data movement.
explanation.tradeoffs: Rebalancing moves data over the network, which consumes bandwidth and can temporarily impact performance. Moving the minimum necessary data (requirement 3) is important — a naive approach that moves all data is prohibitively expensive. This is why 'hash mod N' is terrible for rebalancing.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Rebalancing moves partitions between nodes to maintain fair distribution. Key requirements: fair result, continued service during the process, and minimal data movement.
explanation.commonMistake: Confusing rebalancing (moving partitions between nodes) with repartitioning (changing how data is divided into partitions). Rebalancing moves existing partitions; repartitioning creates new partition boundaries.

prompt.context:
A junior engineer proposes a simple partitioning scheme: assign each key to partition number hash(key) mod N, where N is the number of nodes.

With 10 nodes, key 'alice' hashes to 3, going to node 3.

You add an 11th node (N changes from 10 to 11).
prompt.question: Why is 'hash mod N' a terrible rebalancing strategy?

options.label: Changing N reassigns most keys to different partitions — nearly all data must move
options.description: hash(key) mod 10 ≠ hash(key) mod 11 for most keys, so most keys change partition

options.label: Hash mod N can't handle more than 256 nodes
options.description: The modulo operation overflows for large N

options.label: Hash mod N produces uneven distribution
options.description: The modulo operation clusters keys on certain partitions

explanation.reasoning: When N changes from 10 to 11, hash(key) mod 10 produces a different result than hash(key) mod 11 for the vast majority of keys. For example, if hash('alice') = 123, then 123 mod 10 = 3 but 123 mod 11 = 2 — alice must move from node 3 to node 2. This happens for roughly (N-1)/N of all keys: ~90% of data must move when adding just one node. This violates the 'minimal data movement' requirement.
explanation.tradeoffs: The correct approaches — fixed partition count, dynamic partitioning, proportional to nodes — all ensure that adding a node only moves a proportional fraction of data (roughly 1/N of total data). Hash mod N moves nearly everything, making it prohibitively expensive for large datasets.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Hash mod N is terrible for rebalancing because changing N causes most keys to be reassigned, requiring nearly all data to move. Good strategies move only ~1/N of data when adding a node.
explanation.commonMistake: Using hash mod N because it seems simple and intuitive. It works fine if N never changes, but any cluster size change triggers a near-total data reshuffle.

prompt.context:
Riak, Elasticsearch, Couchbase, and Voldemort use a 'fixed number of partitions' strategy:

1. Create many more partitions than nodes at the start (e.g., 1000 partitions for 10 nodes = 100 per node)
2. When a new node joins, it takes some partitions from existing nodes
3. When a node leaves, its partitions are distributed to remaining nodes

The number of partitions never changes — only the assignment of partitions to nodes changes.
prompt.question: Why create many more partitions than nodes?

options.label: Having excess partitions allows rebalancing by simply reassigning whole partitions — no splitting or merging needed
options.description: Moving whole partitions between nodes is simple and only moves 1/N of data when adding a node

options.label: More partitions improve query performance by increasing parallelism
options.description: Each query touches more partitions, enabling more parallel work

options.label: The extra partitions serve as hot standbys for failover
options.description: Unused partitions take over when active partitions fail

explanation.reasoning: With 1000 partitions and 10 nodes, each node has ~100 partitions. When node 11 joins, it takes ~91 partitions (one from each existing node), resulting in ~91 partitions per node. Only the moved partitions' data transfers — roughly 1/11 of total data. The number of partitions stays fixed at 1000; only the partition-to-node mapping changes. This is simple, predictable, and moves minimal data.
explanation.tradeoffs: The partition count must be chosen carefully at creation time. Too few: can't distribute across many nodes. Too many: each partition is small, adding management overhead. The 'right' number depends on the expected maximum cluster size and data volume — and it can't be changed later (without major rework) in most implementations.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Fixed partition count: create many partitions upfront, assign them to nodes. Rebalancing moves whole partitions between nodes — simple, predictable, and moves only ~1/N of data.
explanation.commonMistake: Choosing the fixed partition count too low or too high. Too low means you can't scale to more nodes later. Too high means excessive overhead per partition (memory, file handles, etc.).

prompt.context:
You're setting up an Elasticsearch cluster with a fixed number of shards (partitions). The data will grow from 10 GB today to potentially 10 TB over the next 3 years. The cluster will grow from 3 nodes to possibly 100 nodes.

You must choose the fixed shard count now.
prompt.question: What is the challenge of choosing the right fixed partition count?

options.label: Too few partitions limits future scalability; too many creates overhead now — you must predict the future cluster size
options.description: The count is fixed at creation and hard to change; you need to balance current overhead against future needs

options.label: No challenge — you can always change the partition count later
options.description: Elasticsearch allows easy shard count changes on existing indices

options.label: The partition count doesn't affect scalability
options.description: Number of partitions is independent of cluster scaling

explanation.reasoning: With fixed partition count, you must choose wisely at creation: if you create 10 partitions, you can never distribute across more than 10 nodes (each node needs at least one partition). If you create 10,000 partitions for a 10 GB dataset, each partition is only 1 MB — too small, causing excessive overhead. The right choice depends on predicting the future data size and cluster size, which is inherently uncertain.
explanation.tradeoffs: This is why some databases (HBase, RethinkDB) use dynamic partitioning instead — partitions split and merge as data grows, adapting automatically. But dynamic partitioning has its own complexities (split/merge operations, initial bootstrapping).
explanation.keyTakeaway: Fixed partition count requires predicting future scale at creation time. Too few limits scalability; too many wastes resources. This prediction problem is the main drawback of fixed partitioning.
explanation.commonMistake: Choosing the partition count based on current cluster size rather than anticipated future maximum. Under-provisioning partitions creates a hard ceiling on scalability.

prompt.context:
HBase and RethinkDB use dynamic partitioning:

- When a partition exceeds a configured size (e.g., 10 GB), it automatically splits into two
- When a partition shrinks below a threshold (after deletions), it merges with an adjacent partition
- The number of partitions adapts to the total data volume
prompt.question: What is the advantage over fixed partition count?

options.label: The number of partitions adapts to actual data volume — no need to predict the future at creation time
options.description: Small datasets have few partitions (low overhead); large datasets have many (good distribution)

options.label: Dynamic partitioning is faster because split/merge operations are instant
options.description: Splitting and merging partitions has zero cost

options.label: Dynamic partitioning eliminates the need for rebalancing
options.description: Partitions automatically move to the right nodes

explanation.reasoning: Dynamic partitioning adapts the partition count to the actual data volume. A small dataset has few partitions (low overhead). As data grows, partitions split automatically, maintaining a reasonable partition size. You don't need to predict the future cluster size at creation time. This is analogous to B-trees splitting and merging nodes as data changes.
explanation.tradeoffs: The downside: an empty database starts with one partition, so all writes initially go to one node until the first split. HBase and MongoDB mitigate this with pre-splitting — creating initial partitions on an empty database. Also, split/merge operations are not instant and can temporarily impact performance.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Dynamic partitioning adapts partition count to data volume — no prediction needed. Partitions split when too large and merge when too small, like B-tree nodes.
explanation.commonMistake: Forgetting that dynamic partitioning starts with a single partition. On an empty database, all traffic goes to one node until the data is large enough to trigger the first split.

prompt.context:
You start a new HBase table with dynamic partitioning. The table is empty. All initial writes go to a single partition on a single node. The other 9 nodes in the cluster are idle.

This will continue until the single partition grows large enough to split.
prompt.question: How do you fix this cold-start problem?

options.label: Pre-splitting: configure an initial set of partition boundaries on the empty table
options.description: Create multiple partitions from the start, spread across nodes, even before data arrives

options.label: Use a larger cluster so the single partition isn't a bottleneck
options.description: More powerful hardware handles the initial load on one node

options.label: Batch-load data all at once to trigger immediate splitting
options.description: Loading a large batch forces the partition to split quickly

explanation.reasoning: Pre-splitting creates multiple partitions on an empty table before any data arrives. You specify initial partition boundaries (which requires some knowledge of expected key distribution). These empty partitions are spread across cluster nodes, so writes are distributed from the start. Both HBase and MongoDB support pre-splitting for dynamic partitioning.
explanation.tradeoffs: Pre-splitting requires knowing enough about the key distribution to choose good initial boundaries. If the boundaries are poorly chosen, some partitions will be empty while others are overloaded. But even imperfect pre-splitting is much better than starting with one partition.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Pre-splitting mitigates dynamic partitioning's cold-start problem by creating multiple partitions on an empty database, ensuring writes are distributed from the beginning.
explanation.commonMistake: Starting a dynamically partitioned table without pre-splitting on a large cluster. All initial writes bottleneck on one node until the first split — potentially for hours depending on write volume.

prompt.context:
Cassandra uses a third approach: partitioning proportional to the number of nodes. Each node has a fixed number of partitions (e.g., 256). When a new node joins, it randomly splits 256 existing partitions and takes half of each split.

With 10 nodes: 2560 partitions. With 11 nodes: 2816 partitions.
prompt.question: How does this compare to fixed partition count?

options.label: Partition count grows with the cluster — no need to predict the right number upfront, and each partition stays a reasonable size
options.description: More nodes = more partitions, keeping partition sizes stable as the cluster grows

options.label: It's identical to fixed partition count, just with a different number
options.description: The behavior is the same; only the initial count differs

options.label: Proportional partitioning eliminates the need for data movement during rebalancing
options.description: New nodes create new partitions without moving existing data

explanation.reasoning: With fixed partition count, the partition size grows as total data grows (since partition count is constant). With proportional-to-nodes partitioning, adding a node adds partitions — keeping the partition size stable. You don't need to predict the future cluster size at creation time. When a new node joins, it splits existing partitions by randomly choosing split points, taking ownership of half the split data.
explanation.tradeoffs: The random split point selection can produce uneven partitions. Also, splitting a partition requires reading and redistributing its data, which is I/O intensive. Cassandra later moved to a more predictable token-range approach. But the core idea — partition count proportional to cluster size — avoids both the prediction problem (fixed) and the cold-start problem (dynamic).
explanation.keyTakeaway: Proportional-to-nodes partitioning (Cassandra): partition count grows with the cluster. Each node has a fixed number of partitions, so partition sizes stay stable as the cluster grows.
explanation.commonMistake: Confusing fixed-total-partitions with fixed-per-node-partitions. Fixed total means partition sizes grow with data. Fixed per node means partition count grows with nodes, keeping sizes stable.

prompt.context:
Your database supports fully automatic rebalancing — it detects uneven load and moves partitions between nodes without human intervention.

A node becomes slow due to overload. The automatic rebalancer decides this node is 'overloaded' and starts moving partitions away from it.

This increases network load on the already-struggling node (it must send partition data over the network while serving requests). The node becomes even slower.
prompt.question: Why can fully automatic rebalancing be dangerous?

options.label: It can cascade: rebalancing an overloaded node adds MORE load (data transfer), making it slower, triggering MORE rebalancing
options.description: Combined with automatic failure detection, it creates a feedback loop that can take down the cluster

options.label: Automatic rebalancing uses too much CPU for the decision-making algorithm
options.description: The rebalancing algorithm itself is computationally expensive

options.label: Automatic rebalancing can't account for time-of-day traffic patterns
options.description: It rebalances for current load without predicting future patterns

explanation.reasoning: Fully automatic rebalancing combined with automatic failure detection can create dangerous feedback loops. A temporarily overloaded node triggers rebalancing, which adds network I/O to the already-struggling node. This makes it even slower, potentially triggering the failure detector to declare it dead. Now a 'failed' node triggers massive rebalancing, overwhelming other nodes, cascading the failure across the cluster.
explanation.tradeoffs: Couchbase, Riak, and Voldemort generate a suggested partition reassignment automatically but require an administrator to confirm before executing. This human-in-the-loop approach is slower but prevents cascading failures from automated decisions. It's a trade-off between recovery speed and safety.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Fully automatic rebalancing can cascade with failure detection: rebalancing an overloaded node adds load, making it slower, triggering more rebalancing. Many systems require human confirmation before executing rebalancing.
explanation.commonMistake: Enabling fully automatic rebalancing without understanding the interaction with failure detection. The combination can turn a minor node overload into a cluster-wide cascading failure.

prompt.context:
A client wants to read key 'alice' from your partitioned database. The cluster has 10 nodes, each holding different partitions.

Three possible routing approaches:
- A: Client connects to any node; that node forwards the request to the correct partition's node
- B: Client connects to a routing tier (load balancer) that knows which partition is where
- C: Client itself knows the partition assignment and connects directly to the correct node
prompt.question: What is this problem — figuring out which node to contact — called?

options.label: Service discovery / request routing — determining which node holds a given partition
options.description: The problem of mapping a key to the node that currently stores its partition

options.label: Load balancing — distributing requests evenly across nodes
options.description: Ensuring no node gets more requests than others

options.label: DNS resolution — translating partition names to network addresses
options.description: Converting logical partition identifiers to IP addresses

explanation.reasoning: Request routing (or service discovery for partitions) is the problem of determining which node currently holds a given partition. After rebalancing, partitions may have moved — clients need an up-to-date mapping. All three approaches (any-node forwarding, routing tier, partition-aware client) solve this problem differently.
explanation.tradeoffs: This is fundamentally a consensus problem: all participants must agree on the current partition-to-node assignment. Changes during rebalancing must propagate to whoever is making routing decisions. Different databases use different solutions depending on their architecture.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Request routing is the problem of mapping keys to the node holding their partition. Three approaches: any-node forwarding, dedicated routing tier, or partition-aware client.
explanation.commonMistake: Confusing request routing with load balancing. Load balancing distributes requests across nodes for even utilization. Request routing ensures each request reaches the CORRECT node for its data.

prompt.context:
HBase, SolrCloud, and Kafka all use Apache ZooKeeper for request routing:

1. Each node registers itself with ZooKeeper and reports which partitions it owns
2. ZooKeeper maintains the authoritative partition-to-node mapping
3. The routing tier (or clients) subscribes to ZooKeeper for changes
4. When partitions are reassigned (rebalancing), ZooKeeper notifies all subscribers
prompt.question: Why is ZooKeeper well-suited for this role?

options.label: ZooKeeper provides a reliable, consistent coordination service with change notifications — solving the consensus problem of partition assignment
options.description: It maintains an authoritative mapping and immediately notifies subscribers when it changes

options.label: ZooKeeper is faster than the databases themselves for key lookups
options.description: ZooKeeper's data store is optimized for fast reads

options.label: ZooKeeper can store the actual partition data, not just metadata
options.description: ZooKeeper serves as a secondary data store for partitions

explanation.reasoning: ZooKeeper is a distributed coordination service that maintains small amounts of metadata reliably and consistently. It tracks which partitions are assigned to which nodes and notifies all subscribers immediately when the mapping changes. This solves the consensus problem: all routers/clients get a consistent, up-to-date view of partition assignments. LinkedIn's Espresso, HBase, SolrCloud, and Kafka all rely on ZooKeeper for this.
explanation.tradeoffs: ZooKeeper is an additional infrastructure dependency — it must be deployed, monitored, and maintained separately. Some databases (Cassandra, Riak) avoid this dependency by using a gossip protocol instead, trading consistency for operational simplicity.
explanation.keyTakeaway: ZooKeeper solves the partition routing problem by maintaining an authoritative, consistent partition-to-node mapping with push notifications to subscribers when assignments change.
explanation.commonMistake: Thinking ZooKeeper stores application data. It only stores small amounts of metadata (partition assignments, leader elections, configuration). The actual database data stays on the partition nodes.

prompt.context:
Cassandra and Riak take a different approach: no external coordination service. Instead, they use a gossip protocol:

- Each node communicates directly with other nodes
- Nodes share partition assignment information through peer-to-peer gossip
- Any node can answer: 'which node owns key X?'
- A client can connect to any node, and that node routes the request
prompt.question: What is the advantage of the gossip approach over ZooKeeper?

options.label: No external coordination service dependency — fewer infrastructure components to deploy and manage
options.description: The database is self-contained; no need to operate a separate ZooKeeper cluster

options.label: Gossip is always faster than ZooKeeper for routing decisions
options.description: Peer-to-peer communication is inherently faster than centralized coordination

options.label: Gossip provides stronger consistency guarantees for partition assignment
options.description: All nodes always agree on the exact partition mapping

explanation.reasoning: The gossip approach eliminates the dependency on an external coordination service like ZooKeeper. This means fewer components to deploy, configure, monitor, and maintain. Cassandra and Riak can be deployed as standalone clusters without additional infrastructure. Clients connect to any node, which knows the current partition assignment and forwards the request appropriately.
explanation.tradeoffs: Gossip is eventually consistent — during rebalancing, different nodes may temporarily have different views of the partition assignment, causing brief misrouting. ZooKeeper provides stronger consistency for the mapping (all subscribers see the same assignment at the same time). The trade-off is operational simplicity vs routing consistency.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Gossip-based routing (Cassandra, Riak) avoids external dependencies like ZooKeeper, simplifying operations. The trade-off is eventually consistent partition assignment — brief misrouting during changes.
explanation.commonMistake: Assuming gossip-based routing is strictly better because it's simpler. ZooKeeper provides stronger consistency for partition assignments, which matters during rebalancing and failover.

prompt.context: After a rebalancing operation, partition 7 has moved from Node A to Node B. A client (or routing tier) still has the old mapping and sends a request for partition 7 to Node A.
prompt.question: Why is keeping the routing information up-to-date fundamentally a consensus/coordination problem?

options.label: All routing participants must agree on the current partition assignment — disagreement causes misrouted requests
options.description: Achieving agreement on the mapping across all clients/routers requires distributed consensus

options.label: Routing tables are too large to fit in memory, requiring distributed storage
options.description: The size of routing data exceeds single-node capacity

options.label: Network latency makes it impossible to route requests quickly
options.description: The speed of routing decisions is the fundamental challenge

explanation.reasoning: All participants in the routing process (clients, routing tiers, or nodes themselves) must have a consistent view of which partitions are on which nodes. If they disagree — one thinks partition 7 is on Node A while another thinks it's on Node B — requests get misrouted. Ensuring agreement across distributed participants is the definition of a consensus problem. ZooKeeper solves this with a consensus protocol; gossip provides eventual agreement.
explanation.tradeoffs: Strict consensus (ZooKeeper) provides immediate consistency but adds latency and a dependency. Gossip provides eventual consistency — during the brief period after rebalancing, some requests may be misrouted. Most databases handle this by having the incorrect node forward the request to the correct one, masking the temporary inconsistency.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Request routing is fundamentally a consensus problem: all participants must agree on the current partition-to-node mapping. Different databases solve this with different consistency guarantees.
explanation.commonMistake: Thinking request routing is a simple lookup problem. In a dynamic system where partitions move between nodes, keeping the routing information consistent across all participants is a distributed coordination challenge.

prompt.context:
Many distributed databases support a 'partition-aware' client library. The client maintains its own copy of the partition assignment map and connects directly to the correct node — no intermediate routing tier.

Examples: Cassandra drivers, MongoDB drivers with shard awareness.
prompt.question: What is the advantage of a partition-aware client?

options.label: Eliminates the extra network hop through a routing tier — the client connects directly to the correct node
options.description: Lower latency and fewer components: client → correct node (1 hop instead of 2)

options.label: The client can cache all partition data locally for offline access
options.description: Partition-aware clients work without network connectivity

options.label: The client can modify partition assignments directly
options.description: Clients with partition awareness can trigger rebalancing

explanation.reasoning: A partition-aware client maintains its own copy of the partition-to-node mapping and connects directly to the correct node. This eliminates the extra network hop through a routing tier (load balancer or proxy), reducing latency. The client subscribes to mapping updates (via ZooKeeper or gossip) to stay current after rebalancing.
explanation.tradeoffs: The trade-off is client complexity — the client library must handle partition discovery, maintain the mapping, handle node failures and rebalancing, and reconnect when mappings change. This is more complex than connecting to a simple load balancer, but the latency savings are significant for high-throughput applications.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Partition-aware clients connect directly to the correct node (no routing tier hop), reducing latency at the cost of more complex client-side logic.
explanation.commonMistake: Using a simple round-robin load balancer in front of a partitioned database. The load balancer doesn't know which node holds which partition, so requests often land on the wrong node and need forwarding — adding unnecessary latency.

prompt.context:
You're comparing the overall architectural approaches of several databases:

- HBase: ZooKeeper for coordination, dynamic partitioning, key-range
- Cassandra: Gossip protocol, proportional-to-nodes partitioning, hash-based
- Elasticsearch: ZooKeeper-less (own coordination), fixed partition count, term-based routing
- MongoDB: Config servers (similar role to ZooKeeper), dynamic partitioning, choice of hash or range
prompt.question: What observation can you make about these databases' partitioning architectures?

options.label: Each database makes different trade-offs across partitioning strategy, rebalancing, and routing — there is no single 'best' combination
options.description: The choices are interconnected but each database optimizes for different workloads and operational models

options.label: They all converge on the same architecture — the differences are superficial
options.description: Under the hood, all partitioned databases work the same way

options.label: Newer databases always use better approaches than older ones
options.description: The architectures represent an evolutionary progression from worst to best

explanation.reasoning: Each database makes a unique combination of trade-offs: key-range vs hash partitioning (range scans vs even distribution), fixed vs dynamic vs proportional rebalancing (simplicity vs adaptability), ZooKeeper vs gossip routing (consistency vs operational simplicity). These choices are driven by the target workload, consistency requirements, and operational philosophy. There is no universally best combination.
explanation.tradeoffs: HBase optimizes for range scans (BigTable lineage). Cassandra optimizes for write throughput and operational simplicity (no ZooKeeper). Elasticsearch optimizes for search workloads (scatter/gather is the normal pattern). MongoDB provides flexibility (choose hash or range). Understanding these trade-offs helps you choose the right database for your specific needs.
explanation.keyTakeaway: Partitioning, rebalancing, and routing strategies are interconnected trade-offs. Each database makes different choices optimized for different workloads — there is no one-size-fits-all solution.
explanation.commonMistake: Choosing a database based on popularity without understanding its partitioning trade-offs. A database optimized for range scans (HBase) may be a poor fit for a workload dominated by point lookups on hash-distributed keys.
